# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of significant epicardial coronary artery stenosis [1]. First described in detail by Tambe and colleagues in 1972, the phenomenon was initially regarded as a curiosity but is now recognized as a clinically relevant cause of recurrent chest pain and acute coronary events [1,2]. Although frequently underdiagnosed, CSFP carries implications for quality of life, recurrent hospitalization, and rarely, life-threatening arrhythmias [3].

## Definition and Diagnosis

CSFP is most reproducibly quantified using the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count method introduced by Gibson et al., which provides an objective, reproducible measure of coronary flow [4]. A corrected TIMI frame count exceeding two standard deviations above the established normal range is generally used to define slow flow [5]. CSFP should be distinguished from coronary no-reflow, which typically occurs in the setting of percutaneous coronary intervention or acute myocardial infarction [6]. The prevalence among patients undergoing angiography for suspected ischemia ranges from 1% to 7% [7].

## Epidemiology and Clinical Presentation

CSFP predominantly affects young to middle-aged men, frequently smokers, and patients with metabolic risk factors [7,8]. The most common presentation is recurrent angina, often at rest, leading to repeated emergency department visits and angiographic evaluation [3,8]. A subset of patients present with acute coronary syndromes, and ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death have been reported, underscoring the potential severity of the condition [9]. Patients commonly demonstrate transient electrocardiographic changes during episodes of chest pain [10].

## Pathophysiology

The pathophysiology of CSFP remains incompletely understood and is likely multifactorial. Microvascular dysfunction is regarded as a central mechanism, supported by impaired coronary flow reserve and abnormal microvascular resistance [11,12]. Endothelial dysfunction, reflected by reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and elevated endothelin-1 levels, has been consistently demonstrated [13,14]. Histopathological studies of myocardial biopsies have revealed small-vessel disease with fibromuscular hyperplasia, myointimal proliferation, and endothelial degeneration [15].

Inflammation has emerged as an important contributor, with elevated levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and other inflammatory markers reported in affected patients [16,17]. Oxidative stress and an imbalance between oxidant and antioxidant systems are also implicated [18]. Additionally, subclinical diffuse atherosclerosis, even in angiographically smooth arteries, may impair flow [19]. Abnormalities in platelet function and increased mean platelet volume have been described, suggesting a prothrombotic tendency [20]. Some investigators have linked CSFP to anatomical factors and increased epicardial fat [21].

## Associated Conditions and Risk Factors

CSFP has been associated with metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia [22]. Hyperhomocysteinemia and elevated uric acid levels have been reported as potential markers [23]. Associations with obstructive sleep apnea and autonomic dysfunction, including altered heart rate variability, have also been described, suggesting a systemic vascular dysregulation [24].

## Prognosis

Although historically considered benign, accumulating evidence indicates that CSFP is associated with significant morbidity. Recurrent angina substantially impairs quality of life, and a measurable proportion of patients experience major adverse cardiac events on long-term follow-up [3,25]. The phenomenon has also been linked to electrical instability, with prolonged QT dispersion and increased risk of arrhythmias [9,25].

## Management

There is no established consensus treatment for CSFP, and management remains largely empirical [26]. Dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, particularly dipyridamole and mibefradil in earlier studies, have shown improvement in TIMI frame counts and symptoms [26]. Nebivolol, a beta-blocker with nitric oxide–potentiating properties, has demonstrated benefit on coronary flow and endothelial function [27]. Statins may improve endothelial function and reduce inflammation independent of lipid lowering [28]. Trimetazidine, a metabolic agent, has been reported to reduce anginal episodes [29]. Lifestyle modification, including smoking cessation and management of metabolic risk factors, remains foundational [30]. Antiplatelet therapy is often employed, although robust randomized evidence is lacking across all therapeutic strategies [30].

## Conclusion

The coronary slow flow phenomenon is an increasingly recognized clinical entity that bridges microvascular dysfunction, endothelial impairment, and inflammation. While it is no longer regarded as wholly benign, the absence of large randomized trials limits evidence-based management. Future research should focus on standardized diagnostic criteria, elucidation of unifying pathophysiological mechanisms, and rigorous evaluation of targeted therapies to improve outcomes for affected patients.
